(CNN) — The speculation is beginning to wear thin: Who will Barack Obama choose to run with him as vice president?

Sen. Barack Obama is set to hold a major event on Saturday, raising the question of whether his running mate — male or female — will appear with him. Time is running short, since the Democratic vice presidential nominee is scheduled to give a prominent speech next Wednesday. That means the announcement could come within days, or possibly within just hours. Each day has seemed like it might finally be the one when the guessing ends.

The Obama campaign even joked about the intense vice presidential chatter on Wednesday, sending reporters an e-mail with the subject line “Vice presidential ...” The message opened with: “Just kidding.” Instead of revealing anything about potential running mates, the e-mail simply listed details of Obama’s schedule.

If the leading candidates know what is happening, however, they are not letting on. Sen. Joe Biden told reporters waiting outside his home in Delaware on Tuesday that he was not the choice.

“You got better things to do, guys; I’m not the guy,” Biden said.

When asked where he would be Saturday — the day Obama is reportedly expected to hold a campaign event in Springfield, Illinois, possibly with his newly chosen running mate — Biden answered, “here,” while pointing toward his driveway. Later that evening, he struck a slightly gentler tone, telling reporters, “I promise you, I don’t know anything.”

Biden, Indiana Sen. Evan Bayh and Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine are widely viewed as being in the top group of possible vice presidential picks.

Bayh has largely avoided attention this week. Whether that means he is trying to sidestep questions is unclear. Over the weekend, he appeared on the Sunday talk shows and seemed to audition for the role of campaign attack dog, going after Republican John McCain over Georgia, Iraq and national security. When asked about the vice presidential race, the former governor said he had “nothing to report today.”

Kaine, by contrast, appears comfortable stepping into the spotlight. Though he is still relatively new to national politics, he is scheduled to appear with Obama on Thursday as the presumptive Democratic nominee campaigns in central Virginia. That has prompted questions about whether Kaine could be unveiled as Obama’s running mate.

The two are set to hold an invitation-only town hall meeting Thursday in Chesterfield County, near Richmond. Kaine’s strong showing in the traditionally conservative suburbs around Richmond helped propel him to the Virginia governorship in 2005.

Obama is scheduled to campaign in Virginia on Wednesday and Thursday before heading back to Illinois for the Springfield event, which will be held at the site where he launched his presidential campaign. That gathering will also begin a tour through battleground states ahead of next week’s Democratic convention in Denver, Colorado.

Obama’s campaign has not disclosed either the timing of the announcement or the identity of the running mate. Officials would not confirm or deny whether Obama will appear with his vice presidential choice over the weekend.

Although much of the recent attention has centered on Bayh, Biden and Kaine, several other serious possibilities remain, and an unexpected selection is still possible. Other prominent names believed to be under consideration include retired Gen. Wesley Clark, New York Sen. Hillary Clinton, Connecticut Sen. Chris Dodd, Texas Rep. Chet Edwards, Nebraska Sen. Chuck Hagel, Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine, former Georgia Sen. Sam Nunn, Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, New Mexico Gov. Bill Richardson and Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius.

Obama’s campaign has said that once he makes his decision, supporters will be notified by text message and e-mail about who will join him on the ticket.

**Obama VP speculation intensifies as campaign prepares text-message announcement**  
*August 2008*

WASHINGTON — With the Democratic National Convention days away, speculation over Barack Obama’s running mate has reached a fever pitch, as supporters, reporters and political operatives wait for a promised text-message announcement from the campaign.

Obama’s team has said it will reveal the vice presidential choice directly to supporters by text message and e-mail, a move intended to showcase the campaign’s vast grassroots network and its reliance on new technology. The announcement is expected before Obama appears with his running mate at a rally in Springfield, Illinois, the city where he launched his presidential campaign in February 2007.

The planned event has only heightened interest in the decision, with several names continuing to dominate the discussion: Sen. Joe Biden of Delaware, Sen. Evan Bayh of Indiana and Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine.

Biden, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, is widely viewed as a leading contender because of his long experience in Washington and his foreign policy credentials. Obama, a first-term senator from Illinois, has faced repeated criticism from Republican John McCain’s campaign over his readiness to be commander in chief. Biden could help answer those attacks, though his decades in the Senate and occasional off-the-cuff remarks could complicate Obama’s message of change.

Bayh, a former Indiana governor and two-term senator, is seen as a more centrist option who could help Obama appeal to working-class and independent voters in the Midwest. Indiana, normally Republican in presidential elections, has drawn renewed Democratic interest this year, and Bayh’s political organization in the state is considered strong. Supporters say his governing experience and moderate profile would balance the ticket.

Kaine, an early Obama supporter and the governor of a key battleground state, has also remained part of the conversation. Virginia has not voted Democratic for president since 1964, but the Obama campaign believes demographic changes and an energized Democratic base could put the state in play. Kaine’s allies point to his executive experience, his appeal to faith-based voters and his close personal rapport with Obama.

Other names have circulated in recent weeks, but the final phase of the search appears to have narrowed attention to a small group. The campaign has kept the process tightly controlled, with advisers offering little public guidance and declining to confirm reports about finalists.

The secrecy has fueled an around-the-clock guessing game. News crews have watched airports, homes and Senate offices for signs of unusual movement, while supporters have signed up online to receive the campaign’s text alert. The approach reflects Obama’s broader strategy of building a direct line to millions of voters, bypassing traditional media filters while generating suspense around one of the most important decisions of his campaign.

The vice presidential choice comes at a pivotal moment. Obama is preparing to accept the Democratic nomination in Denver after a long primary fight against Sen. Hillary Clinton. While party leaders have worked to unify Democrats, McCain has sought to portray Obama as inexperienced and untested on national security.

Whoever joins the ticket will be expected to help Obama broaden his appeal, sharpen the campaign’s argument against McCain and reassure voters still weighing whether the Illinois senator is ready for the presidency.

For now, the political world is waiting for a message — one that could arrive first not on television, but on millions of cell phones.

**Obama nears running-mate decision as Democratic convention approaches**

As Barack Obama moves toward formally accepting the Democratic presidential nomination, his campaign is closing in on one of the most consequential choices of the general election: who will join him on the ticket.

The decision, expected before the Democratic convention, has become the subject of intense speculation in Washington and beyond, with Democrats watching for clues about whether Obama will prioritize governing experience, foreign policy credentials, geographic balance or a symbolic show of party unity after a bruising primary fight with Hillary Clinton.

Obama has kept the process tightly controlled, saying little publicly about the finalists while aides have worked to preserve secrecy around the vetting operation. The campaign has signaled only that the Illinois senator is looking for someone who is “ready to be president” and who shares his vision for changing the direction of the country.

Among the names most frequently mentioned are Delaware Sen. Joe Biden, Indiana Sen. Evan Bayh, Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine, Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius and Clinton, whose supporters have continued to press for her consideration after she won millions of votes in the Democratic primaries.

Biden, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has long been seen as a strong potential complement to Obama because of his decades of experience on national security and foreign affairs — areas Republicans have argued are Obama’s vulnerabilities. But Biden has repeatedly downplayed the possibility.

“I am not the guy,” Biden told reporters when asked about his chances, while also praising Obama and making clear he would support the ticket. At other points, Biden has joked about the speculation and suggested he was not campaigning for the role.

Still, Democrats close to the process say Biden’s experience, working-class roots and ability to take the fight to Republicans make him a serious contender. His long Senate record, however, would also bring scrutiny, including past presidential campaign controversies and his vote to authorize the Iraq War — an issue central to Obama’s rise.

Bayh, a former Indiana governor and two-term senator, is viewed as a safe and disciplined option who could help Obama compete in traditionally Republican territory. Kaine, an early Obama supporter and governor of a pivotal battleground state, would reinforce the campaign’s message of generational change. Sebelius could help broaden the ticket’s appeal and has won statewide in heavily Republican Kansas.

Clinton remains the most politically complicated possibility. Choosing her could unify Democrats and energize many of her supporters, but some Obama allies worry it would revive tensions from the primary and complicate the campaign’s message of moving beyond the politics of the 1990s.

The timing of the announcement is also being carefully choreographed. Obama’s campaign is expected to use the selection to generate momentum heading into the convention, where Democrats hope to present a unified front against Republican Sen. John McCain.

McCain’s campaign, meanwhile, is preparing to seize on the choice no matter who it is — either by arguing Obama needed a seasoned Washington figure to compensate for his inexperience or by portraying the selection as a political calculation.

For Obama, the decision is a defining test of judgment. After months of campaigning on change, he must now choose the person who would stand one heartbeat from the presidency — and who could help shape voters’ first clear impression of the Democratic ticket heading into the fall.

With the Democratic National Convention days away, Barack Obama is entering the final stretch of one of the most closely watched decisions of his presidential campaign: the selection of a vice-presidential running mate.

Obama’s campaign has been carefully managing the suspense, signaling that the announcement could come at any moment while directing supporters to sign up to receive the news first by text message or email. The strategy reflects both the campaign’s intense message discipline and its broader effort to use technology to build a direct connection with voters — bypassing the traditional news cycle and turning a major political announcement into an organizing tool.

The decision comes as Obama prepares for a series of public appearances that may offer clues, or perhaps deliberate misdirection, about his choice. He is scheduled to campaign in Virginia, a traditionally Republican-leaning state that Democrats believe could be competitive in November, before heading to Springfield, Illinois, the city where he launched his presidential bid in 2007 and where his campaign has planned a major event tied to the vice-presidential rollout.

The Virginia stop has fueled speculation about Gov. Tim Kaine, a close Obama ally and one of the names most frequently mentioned in the running-mate search. Kaine, a former mayor of Richmond and a Catholic fluent in Spanish, was an early Obama supporter and has been viewed inside Democratic circles as a figure who could reinforce Obama’s message of generational change and pragmatic governance. His presence in a battleground state could also help Democrats compete more aggressively in Virginia, which has not voted for a Democratic presidential nominee since 1964.

But Kaine is not the only Democrat drawing attention. Sen. Evan Bayh of Indiana has been the subject of persistent speculation, particularly among those who believe Obama may seek a more centrist, Midwestern figure with executive experience. Bayh, a former two-term governor and the son of a prominent Democratic senator, could potentially help Obama appeal to working-class and moderate voters in states across the industrial Midwest. His supporters argue that he would bring discipline, caution and a record of electoral success in Republican territory.

Sen. Joe Biden of Delaware is also widely seen as a leading contender. Biden, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, would bring decades of Washington experience and deep credentials on foreign policy and national security — areas where Republicans have sought to portray Obama as inexperienced. Biden’s defenders say he could serve as an effective attack dog against the Republican ticket and reassure voters who want a more seasoned hand alongside the first-term senator from Illinois. His critics, however, note that his long record and unscripted speaking style could complicate Obama’s tightly controlled campaign message.

The Obama team has kept the process unusually guarded. Advisers have disclosed little publicly about the search, and the campaign has worked to maintain suspense while minimizing leaks. The result has been a wave of speculation from Democrats, reporters and party insiders, with every campaign stop, chartered flight and schedule change scrutinized for hints.

The planned notification system has added to the sense of anticipation. Supporters have been encouraged to provide their mobile phone numbers and email addresses so they can receive the announcement directly from the campaign. While presidential campaigns have long used major announcements to collect donor and volunteer information, Obama’s use of text messaging marks a more modern approach, consistent with a campaign that has relied heavily on online fundraising, social networking and digital organizing.

The timing is politically significant. Obama is seeking to regain the initiative after a summer in which Republican John McCain and his allies intensified attacks over Obama’s readiness to serve as commander in chief. The vice-presidential selection offers Obama an opportunity to shape several days of coverage heading into the Democratic convention in Denver, where he will formally accept the nomination.

The choice also carries broader strategic implications. A selection such as Biden could be read as an effort to address experience and foreign policy concerns. A pick like Bayh could signal outreach to moderates and voters in the Rust Belt. Choosing Kaine would emphasize personal chemistry, loyalty and the campaign’s theme of change, while potentially underlining the importance of Virginia in Obama’s electoral map.

For now, the campaign is allowing the speculation to build. Obama’s appearances in Virginia and Springfield will be watched closely, not only for what he says but for who appears alongside him and how the campaign stages the events. Springfield, in particular, carries symbolic weight for Obama, linking his vice-presidential announcement to the place where he began his national campaign and to the Lincoln imagery he has often invoked.

Whatever the decision, Obama’s running mate will immediately become a central figure in the general election fight. The new ticket will be expected to unify Democrats after a long primary battle with Hillary Clinton, appeal to undecided voters and help answer Republican criticisms heading into the fall campaign.

Until the text message arrives, however, the guessing game continues.
